In summary, our research is concerned with
PTEN, a tumor suppressor gene with multiple functions and with AKT, an important downstream effector of PI3K that is activated in a large number of human cancers.
the understanding of the role of AKT in PTEN tumorigenic pathways and the identification of new AKT-independent mechanisms.
the role of PTEN in tumorigenesis and its interaction with other oncogenetic pathways.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
PTEN is more than the AKTs pathway.
PTEN is more than an AKT pathway.
PTEN tumorigenic activity requires the presence of an activated AKT pathway but that the AKT pathway alone is not sufficient to induce tumors.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
PTEN is more than the AKTP3K pathway and that the PTEN pathway is more than AKT.
AKT is not the only target of PTEN and that PTEN is more than an AKT inhibitor.
PTEN tumorigenicity is a complex process involving AKT and other pathways.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the PI3K/AKT pathway is a complex network of interacting components and the loss of PTEN is not simply a loss of AKT regulation.
PTEN is not a simple regulator of the AKT pathway, but rather an important player in many other pathways that contribute to tumorigenesis.
AKT and PTEN have to be considered as a complex pathway and not as a single target.
